plain: An ancient Hindu school that splits reality in two: pure consciousness (purusha) and active matter (prakriti). Suffering comes from mixing them up; knowing they are separate frees you.

upanishadic_brahman.note: Its spirit-matter split grows out of Upanishadic distinctions between the self and the material world.

name: Absolute sovereignty
origin_note: Jean Bodin defines sovereignty as the absolute, perpetual and indivisible power of a commonwealth in Les Six livres de la République (1576), written amid the French Wars of Religion
plain: The idea that every state needs one supreme power, above all other laws and bodies, that cannot be split or shared. Only God and natural law stand above it.

rationale.christianity: Binds even the absolute sovereign by divine law, and treats sovereignty as ultimately from God.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Its undivided sovereign clashes with later liberal ideas of divided and limited power.

rationale.hierarchy: Puts one undivided supreme power over all estates, assemblies and subjects.

Shaped English absolutist doctrine in the late 16th and 17th centuries.
Set the terms of German constitutional debates over the Empire's hybrid structure.

aristotelian_teleology.note: Bodin drew on Aristotle's classifications of states and Roman law while building a new concept of sovereignty.

name: Religious right
origin_note: Moral Majority founded June 1979 by Jerry Falwell, pastor of Thomas Road Baptist Church in Lynchburg, Virginia, with Paul Weyrich; the term 'religious right' first gained widespread usage in the late 1970s (Grokipedia, Christian right)
plain: Conservative evangelicals and allied Catholics organizing to vote on abortion, school prayer, marriage and religious liberty.
summary: From the 1979 Moral Majority on, conservative evangelicals became a core Republican voting bloc focused on abortion, family and religious liberty.

rationale.christianity: A coalition of conservative Protestant evangelicals, fundamentalists and some Catholics (Grokipedia, Christian right).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Works through votes and courts and invokes religious liberty, while fighting secular liberal rulings; mixed.
rationale.marxism: Anti-communist, Cold War in origin.
rationale.darwinism: Backs creationism in schools; judgment from fundamentalist inheritance.
rationale.critical_theory: Opposes secular humanism and progressive cultural agendas (Grokipedia, Moral Majority).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).
rationale.nationalism: No real link to Nationalism.
rationale.humor: Earnest register.
rationale.irony: Sincere moral politics.
rationale.abstraction: Argues from scripture and moral concerns, not theory.
rationale.hierarchy: Campaigns for marriage as one man and one woman and for a biblical moral order in law.

places.note: Moral Majority drives targeted Southern Baptists and fundamentalists, many former Carter voters.
White evangelicals gave Trump 81% of their vote in 2016 (Grokipedia, Christian right).

christian_fundamentalism.note: The term described 'a coalition of conservative Protestant evangelicals, fundamentalists, and some Catholics'; Falwell was a Baptist fundamentalist pastor.

party_alignment.note: Grokipedia: Moral Majority turned evangelicals into 'a reliable Republican base'; white evangelicals gave 78% to Romney (2012) and 81% to Trump (2016).

name: New Democrats
origin_note: Democratic Leadership Council founded March 1985 after the 1984 defeat by Al From and Will Marshall; Bill Clinton chaired it from 1990; New Democrat Coalition formed in the House in 1997

rationale.christianity: Secular program; some appeal to community and responsibility.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Liberal on markets and rights; 'opportunity, personal responsibility, and community' (Grokipedia, DLC).
rationale.marxism: Rejects class politics and expansive government programs (Grokipedia, DLC).
rationale.critical_theory: Accused by the left of ignoring identity politics; no link.

rationale.hierarchy: The Third Way puts equality of opportunity over equality of outcome, neither leveling nor defending rank.

places.note: Shaped Clinton's 1992 win and 1990s Democratic platforms; the New Democrat Coalition carries it in the House.
The DLC's influence extended to Tony Blair's policies (Grokipedia, DLC).

new_deal_liberalism.note: Founded by Democrats to steer the party 'toward moderate policies and away from its leftward ideological shift since the late 1960s'.

party_alignment.note: Intra-Democratic faction; the DLC closed in 2011 but the New Democrat Coalition, formed by DLC members in 1997, remains in the House.

name: Democratic socialism in America
origin_note: DSA founded March 1982 at a Detroit convention merging Michael Harrington's Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee and the New American Movement

rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Works through elections: DSA 'emphasized reforming the Democratic Party from within over third-party runs' (Grokipedia, DSA).
rationale.marxism: Rejects Marxism-Leninism (Grokipedia, DSA), yet 'democratic socialism explicitly seeks to supplant capitalism' (Grokipedia, Democratic socialism).
rationale.critical_theory: NAM came from New Left remnants and socialist-feminist groups (Grokipedia, DSA).

social_democracy.note: DSOC under Harrington brought social democrats focused on unions and the Democratic left.

party_alignment.note: Not a party; DSA 'emphasized reforming the Democratic Party from within over third-party runs' (Grokipedia, DSA). Contested inside DSA. The Squad, an informal subgroup of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, overlaps with DSA but is not the same group (Grokipedia, Congressional Progressive Caucus).

rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Rights-based liberal politics, 'seeking to pull the Democratic Party toward more interventionist government roles in the economy and society' (Grokipedia, CPC).

democratic_socialism_us.note: The caucus formed 'with early ties to Democratic Socialists of America'.

party_alignment.note: A Democratic caucus formed 'to pull the Democratic Party toward more interventionist government'. Sanders, a founder, is an independent.

name: Neo-Thomism

The Catholic University of America, founded 1887, adapted it for an immigrant church.

thomism.note: Set out to restore the doctrines and methods of Thomas Aquinas in Catholic schools and seminaries.

name: Neostoicism
origin_note: Justus Lipsius wrote De Constantia in the winter of 1583–84 while teaching at Leiden University during the Dutch Revolt, and published it in 1584; his Politica followed in 1589
plain: A late-1500s revival of Stoic ethics, reshaped to fit Christianity. It taught constancy, steady endurance in times of war and chaos, trusting God's plan instead of the old Stoic idea of fate.

rationale.christianity: Swaps Stoic fate and determinism for God's providence, free will and grace.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Puts order, obedience and religious uniformity ahead of personal liberty.

rationale.darwinism: Comes before Darwinism existed; no link.

Guillaume du Vair's 1594 book on constancy adapted it for royal circles during the wars of religion.
Translations of De Constantia reached courtiers and scholars; Francis Bacon cited it.

stoic_logos.note: Revived ancient Stoic ethics, chiefly from Seneca, and adapted them to Christianity.

renaissance_humanism.note: Humanist recovery and editing of Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius made the revival possible.

name: Modern synthesis
origin_note: Built between the early 1930s and the 1950s by population geneticists and naturalists; Julian Huxley named it in Evolution: The Modern Synthesis (1942)
plain: The mid-1900s merger of Darwin's natural selection with Mendel's genetics. Evolution became a change in how common genes are in a population, driven by mutation, drift, gene flow and selection.
summary: Fisher, Haldane, Wright, Dobzhansky, Mayr and Huxley unite Darwin and Mendel: evolution as shifting gene frequencies, the mid-century core of biology.

rationale.platonism: Mayr's 'Typological versus Population Thinking' (1959) attacked Platonic essentialism in biology (Grokipedia, Ernst Mayr).
rationale.aristotelianism: Stance: rejects goals or purposes built into evolution, the final causes of Aristotle (Grokipedia, Ernst Mayr).
rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: No real link to Enlightenment liberalism.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.darwinism: Makes natural selection, now explained by genetics, the main driver of adaptive evolution.

rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.nationalism: No real link to Nationalism.

rationale.irony: Makes its case directly, without ironic distance.
rationale.abstraction: Explains how life changes through physical genes and the mathematics of populations.
rationale.hierarchy: A scientific theory of how species change; it takes no stand on social rank.

Home of Fisher, Haldane and Huxley, and of field studies in ecological genetics in Oxfordshire.

darwinian_selection.note: Reconciled Darwin's natural selection with Mendel's laws of inheritance.

name: Western Marxism
origin_note: György Lukács, in exile in Vienna, published History and Class Consciousness in 1923, the same year as Karl Korsch's Marxism and Philosophy; Maurice Merleau-Ponty coined the name in 1955
plain: Marxist thinkers in Western Europe from the 1920s who turned from economics to culture and consciousness. They asked why workers' revolutions failed in the West and how capitalism wins consent.
summary: Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci rework Marx through Hegel: reification, hegemony and culture over economic determinism, apart from Soviet orthodoxy.

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Treats liberal, bourgeois ideas as ideology that props up capitalist rule.
rationale.marxism: Marxist theory throughout, though it rejects Soviet-style orthodoxy.
rationale.critical_theory: Shares Critical theory's focus on ideology and culture, and counts the Frankfurt School among its currents.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.nationalism: No real link to Nationalism.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Makes its case directly, without ironic distance.
rationale.abstraction: Keeps Marx's materialism but stresses consciousness and culture; critics call it idealist.
rationale.hierarchy: Aims to end class rule and studies how domination wins consent.

Althusser's structural Marxism took hold, and Marxism peaked in French universities around 1968.
The Italian Communist Party's Eurocommunism adapted Gramsci's idea of hegemony.

marxism.note: A body of Marxist theory that broke from Soviet-style economic determinism.

hegelian_dialectic.note: Its founders turned back to Hegel's dialectics to explain why revolution failed in the West.

name: New Confucianism

plain: A 20th-century movement to renew Confucian thought for the modern world. It keeps the Confucian focus on inner moral growth, but argues that this fits with science and democracy.

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Argues Confucian ethics can support democracy and science, while rejecting Western individualism.
rationale.marxism: Its 1958 manifesto defended Chinese culture against Marxist materialism.
rationale.critical_theory: Comes before Critical theory existed; no link.
rationale.confucianism: Sets out to renew Confucian ethics and metaphysics for modern times.
rationale.buddhism: Engages Buddhist thought; Xiong Shili wove Buddhist ideas into his Confucian system.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.nationalism: No real link to Nationalism.

Revived since the 1980s, with new institutes and classes at Peking and Tsinghua Universities.

neo_confucianism.note: Sees itself as the third epoch of Confucianism after Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism, which it set out to renew.

transcendental_idealism.note: Engaged Kant's philosophy; Mou Zongsan built a moral metaphysics joining Kantian ethics to Confucian thought.

burkean_conservatism.note: Grokipedia speaks of 'one-nation's Burkean inheritance favoring prudence over mass agitation'.

party_alignment_gb.note: The One Nation Group was 'founded in 1950 by nine newly elected Conservative MPs'.

rationale.nationalism: No real link to Nationalism.

rationale.irony: Sincere.

Carr's 1939 critique of interwar idealism appeared in London on the eve of war.

parent_note: Realists also trace their roots to Thucydides, who has no node here, and to Machiavelli's The Prince, which the Machiavellian republicanism node does not cover.

social_contract.note: Hobbes's 'state of nature' in Leviathan (1651) laid 'groundwork for realism's emphasis on systemic insecurity' among states.

name: Latter-day Saint movement
origin_note: The Church of Christ was 'formally organized on April 6, 1830, in Fayette, New York, at the home of Peter Whitmer Sr., with six initial members'; the Book of Mormon was 'published in March 1830 by E. B. Grandin in Palmyra'. Dated here to 1827, when Smith 'retrieved the plates in 1827' near Manchester, New York (Grokipedia, Golden plates); the reported First Vision (1820) precedes it
plain: A Christian movement organized as a church by Joseph Smith in 1830; it teaches a restored church, the Book of Mormon as added scripture, living prophets and temple rites for eternal families.
summary: Restorationist Christian tradition organized as a church by Joseph Smith in 1830: Great Apostasy and restoration, Book of Mormon, embodied God, eternal progression, temples; led west by Brigham Young.

rationale.platonism: Rejects immaterial being: 'There is no such thing as immaterial matter. All spirit is matter' (D&C 131:7).
rationale.christianity: A 'restorationist Christian tradition' centered on Christ; rejects the Nicene Trinity for an embodied Father and Son (Grokipedia, LDS movement; Mormonism).
rationale.gnosticism: Temple rites and saving knowledge lead to exaltation, but matter is good and embodiment sought, the reverse of Gnostic dualism; no Gnostic link shown.
rationale.hermeticism: Smith's early seer-stone treasure seeking is documented as 'vernacular occultism'; a Hermetic lineage is argued by some, not shown (Grokipedia, Mormonism).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Stresses agency and free choice in the plan of salvation; accepted constitutional order after 1890 but built a 'semi-theocratic society' in Utah (Grokipedia).
rationale.marxism: Early communal economics in Utah (Grokipedia, Mormonism), yet the modern church teaches tithing and self-reliance, not class struggle.
rationale.darwinism: Frames human origins through divine creation and eternal progression of spirits (Grokipedia, Mormonism); no Darwinian frame.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).
rationale.judaism: The Book of Mormon tells of migrants 'from Jerusalem around 600 BCE'; adopts Israelite priesthood, temple and covenant language (Grokipedia, LDS movement).
rationale.romanticism: Rose in the revivalist 'Burned-over District' with visions and a sacred American past; romantic in mood, not a Romantic doctrine.
rationale.nationalism: The Book of Mormon makes the Americas a 'promised land' (Grokipedia, Book of Mormon); now global, with most members outside the US.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Makes its case directly, without ironic distance.
rationale.abstraction: Materialist metaphysics: 'All spirit is matter, but it is more fine or pure' (D&C 131:7); God 'has a body of flesh and bones' (Grokipedia, Joseph Smith).
rationale.hierarchy: LDS polity is 'Hierarchical with prophetic leadership' (Grokipedia, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints); callings are lay, 'voluntary and unpaid'.

places.note: Founded amid revivals of the Burned-over District; organized at Fayette in 1830.
Gathering centers until Smith's assassination on June 27, 1844 and the succession crisis.
Brigham Young led the trek west; Young served as church president 'from 1847 until his death'.
International membership is now the majority, e.g. Brazil 'over 1.4 million members'.

protestantism.note: Smith grew up amid revivals where 'Methodists, Baptists, and Presbyterians' competed; his First Vision told him to join none, so the movement defines itself against them.

methodism.note: Stands in for the Second Great Awakening setting (no node yet). Palmyra records show 'Presbyterian and Methodist activities as early as 1816' and a June 1818 camp meeting; no doctrinal link shown.

parent_note: Key ancestors Restorationism (Christian primitivism) and the Second Great Awakening have no nodes on main; proposed, not built. No Hermetic or ceremonial_magic edge: folk-magic and Masonic links are documented only as contested context.

name: Florentine civic humanism
origin_note: Bruni's Laudatio Florentinae Urbis, delivered c. 1403–1404, praised Florence's mixed constitution; Salutati, chancellor 1375–1406, had argued for the active civic life. Hans Baron later named the thesis
plain: The Florentine humanists' belief that studying the classics should train citizens to take an active part in running a free republic.
summary: Humanism turned to republican service in Florence, c. 1403: Salutati and Bruni praised the active civic life, mixed government and liberty against Milanese princely rule.

rationale.platonism: Bruni translated Plato's dialogues, but Florentine civic humanism prized Aristotle's and Cicero's civic ethics over Platonic contemplation.
rationale.aristotelianism: Bruni translated Aristotle's Politics and Ethics and used the mixed constitution to praise Florence (Grokipedia, Leonardo Bruni).
rationale.stoicism: Revived Cicero's ethic of public duty, which borrows Stoic themes; Stoicism is not its source.
rationale.christianity: Salutati held that true virtue and service to God required civic participation (Grokipedia, Coluccio Salutati).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Prized liberty and rule of law against despots, three centuries before Enlightenment liberalism, which it anticipates loosely.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Rated the active civic life above monastic contemplation, though argued through rhetoric and classical learning.
rationale.hierarchy: Praised a mixed constitution, but its humanists were a small educated elite (Grokipedia, Renaissance humanism criticisms).
rationale.nationalism: No documented relation (predates Nationalism).

places.note: Salutati (chancellor 1375–1406) and Bruni (chancellor 1427–1444) carried it in the Florentine chancery.

renaissance_humanism.note: Salutati bridged 'Petrarchan humanism with the civic traditions of the Florentine Republic' and mentored Bruni and Poggio Bracciolini.

aristotelian_teleology.note: Bruni translated Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics into Latin and drew on Polybius, Cicero and Aristotle for Florence's mixed constitution.

parent_note: Hans Baron coined the 'civic humanism' thesis in the 20th century; he is its historian, not a parent. The term is a scholars' label, and Grokipedia's Bruni page notes debate over Baron's interpretation.

name: Machiavellian republicanism
origin_note: Machiavelli composed the Discourses on Livy between 1513 and 1519, in exile after the Florentine Republic fell in 1512
plain: Machiavelli's case for republics: armed citizens, balanced institutions and open conflict between nobles and people keep a free state alive and guard it against corruption.
summary: Republic theory of Machiavelli's Discourses (1513–1519): Roman models, mixed government, citizen militia, and civic virtù against fortune and corruption.

rationale.platonism: Grokipedia records a rejection of idealism; Machiavelli judged states by 'effectual truth', not ideal forms.
rationale.aristotelianism: Adapts Aristotelian and Polybian mixed constitutions, in Pocock's reading (Grokipedia, Discourses on Livy).
rationale.christianity: Replaced divine providence with human contrivance; the Church banned the Discourses (Grokipedia, Discourses on Livy).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Backed popular participation and institutional checks, which later fed Atlantic republicanism, not Lockean rights.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.nietzsche: Recasts virtù as adaptive efficacy against fortune, not moral excellence; a loose echo, not a documented tie to Nietzsche.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Reasoned from Roman history and Florentine experience toward 'effectual truth' (Grokipedia, Niccolò Machiavelli).
rationale.hierarchy: Favored popular participation and the people's guard of liberty against the nobles, within a mixed constitution.
rationale.nationalism: Precursor only: The Prince's call to free Italy from 'the barbarians' is read as proto-nationalist; Risorgimento leaders invoked him.

places.note: Machiavelli founded a citizen militia in 1506 and wrote the Discourses in exile after 1512.
Harrington's Oceana (1656) drew explicitly on the Discourses during the Commonwealth.

florentine_civic_humanism.note: Machiavelli had a humanist education and served the chancery from 1498 to 1512. Grokipedia says he broke from humanism and contrasts him with Bruni; Pocock sees continuity.

parent_note: Guicciardini is listed as a Florentine contemporary in the same debate; Pocock is its historian, not a parent.

name: Country ideology
origin_note: The Country Party arose in the 1670s in the Cavalier Parliament; Cato's Letters (1720–1723) and Bolingbroke's Craftsman (from 1726) gave it its 18th-century voice against Walpole. The 1675 date is approximate; the tradition peaked around 1720 with Cato's Letters
plain: An 18th-century British opposition creed: power corrupts through court patronage, debt and standing armies, so independent landowners and civic virtue must check it.
summary: British 'country' opposition, from the 1670s to its peak against Walpole: anti-corruption, anti-standing-army, anti-debt; carried by Cato's Letters and Bolingbroke.

rationale.aristotelianism: Held civic virtue to be the guard of liberty, an indirect echo of Aristotle's civic ethics.
rationale.christianity: Trenchard and Gordon's Independent Whig critiqued clerical power; Bolingbroke attacked clerical authority (Grokipedia, Cato's Letters; Bolingbroke).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Cato's Letters rested on natural rights 'akin to John Locke's' (Grokipedia, Cato's Letters), close to Enlightenment liberalism.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Worked through weekly polemic and parliamentary campaigns on armies, debt and patronage, not systematic philosophy.
rationale.hierarchy: Attacked court patronage and executive power, but spoke for independent landed gentry; Bolingbroke wanted a Patriot King.
rationale.nationalism: No documented relation (predates Nationalism).

places.note: Peaked in opposition to Walpole in the 1720s–1730s; declined by the 1750s under the Pelhams.
Cato's Letters 'circulated widely and profoundly shaped revolutionary ideology' in the colonies.

classical_republicanism.note: The Country Party drew 'on classical republican and real Whig traditions' in opposing standing armies, national debt and court patronage.

parent_note: Merges the Whig Commonwealthmen (Trenchard, Gordon) with Bolingbroke's Tory-led country opposition, as the Country Party page does.

name: Nominalism
origin_note: Roscelin of Compiègne (c. 1050–1125), 'often regarded as the first explicit nominalist', held universals to be flatus vocis; William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) gave it 'its most influential formulation'
plain: The view that only individual things exist; general words like 'man' or 'rose' name groups of similar things, not real shared natures.
summary: Medieval denial that universals exist outside minds and words, from Roscelin to Ockham's 14th-century system; carries the principle later called Ockham's razor.

rationale.platonism: Rejects Platonist commitments to immaterial forms (Grokipedia, Nominalism).
rationale.aristotelianism: Grew out of scholastic reading of Aristotle's logic but denies the common forms moderate realists drew from him.
rationale.christianity: Worked out by Christian theologians; Ockham was a Franciscan friar writing on theology.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Later linked to early modern empiricism through Hobbes and Locke (Grokipedia, Nominalism); an ancestor at most.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Puts individual things and sense experience ahead of abstract essences, though argued through technical logic.
rationale.hierarchy: Ockham argued lay and clerical rights to resist erroneous papal decrees (Grokipedia, William of Ockham).
rationale.nationalism: No documented relation (predates Nationalism).

places.note: Ockhamist moderni disputed realists at the University of Paris; its arts faculty curbed Ockham's doctrines in 1339.
Ockham began theological training at Oxford by at least 1317.
Ockham lived in Munich under Louis IV from about 1329 until his death on April 9, 1347.

aristotelian_teleology.note: Context, not descent: the link is Aristotle's logic. The universals debate was 'sparked by Porphyry's Isagoge', an introduction to Aristotle's logic.

parent_note: Rival of realism: Thomism (moderate realism) and the via antiqua; Thomism is later (1265) than Roscelin and not a parent.

name: German idealism
origin_note: A movement 'spanning roughly from the 1780s to the 1840s' in response to Kant's Critique of Pure Reason (1781); Fichte built his system at Jena from 1794, where Schelling joined him in 1798
plain: The German philosophers after Kant who held that mind or spirit shapes reality itself, from Fichte's self-positing ego to Hegel's absolute.
summary: Post-Kantian systems of Fichte, Schelling and Hegel, about 1794–1840s, holding that mind constitutes reality; feeds Hegel's dialectic and British and American idealism.

rationale.platonism: Idealism 'traces to Plato's' Forms (Grokipedia, Idealism); a theme, not a documented lineage here.
rationale.christianity: Fichte was dismissed in 1799 over alleged atheism; Hegel studied theology; a loose and contested tie.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Fichte saw the state as a vehicle for ethical progress and cosmopolitan humanity (Grokipedia, German idealism).
rationale.marxism: Its dialectic of history passes to Marxism through Hegelian dialectic, already on the map.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Holds that mind constitutes reality; among the most abstract systems in the map.
rationale.hierarchy: Fichte's later work stressed communal life and the state; mild.
rationale.romanticism: Fichte's lectures and Schelling's nature-philosophy fed Romanticism; Schelling 'profoundly influenced Romanticism'.
rationale.nationalism: Fichte's Addresses to the German Nation urged national identity through language and education, framed in cosmopolitan terms.

places.note: Fichte taught there 1794–1799 and Schelling from 1798.
Fichte's later Berlin writings, 1800–1814, turned to language and communal life.
Left an international legacy in British idealism.
Left an international legacy in American idealism.

transcendental_idealism.note: It 'sought to resolve tensions in Kant's transcendental idealism'; Fichte was shaped by Kant's Critique of Practical Reason in 1789.

spinozism.note: Schelling studied 'the works of Kant, Spinoza, and Fichte' at Tübingen; Spinoza's monism 'inspired later holistic views of reality'.

name: Guelphs
origin_note: Names from Welf and Waiblingen came into Italian use in the late 12th century and 'solidified' as faction labels 'in Florence by 1215'; Guelphs backed the papacy against imperial rule
plain: The medieval Italian faction that sided with the pope against the Holy Roman Emperor, strong in Florence, Genoa and Bologna.
summary: Pro-papal faction of Italian city-states from about 1215 into the 14th century; Florence's Guelphs split into Whites and Blacks around 1300.

rationale.christianity: The pro-papal side in the papacy's dispute with the Empire (Grokipedia, Guelphs and Ghibellines).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: No real link to Enlightenment liberalism.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Alignments were 'pragmatic rather than doctrinal', driven by feuds and trade (Grokipedia, Guelphs and Ghibellines).
rationale.hierarchy: Backed papal authority but also communal autonomy against imperial overlordship.
rationale.nationalism: No documented relation (predates Nationalism).

places.note: A leading Guelph stronghold; split into White and Black Guelphs around 1300.
Aligned with the Guelphs amid maritime rivalry with Ghibelline Pisa.
Predominantly Guelph, siding with papal interests.

roman_catholicism.note: Guelphs were the 'pro-papal' faction; Innocent III 'solidified Guelph ascendancy' against imperial claims.

parent_note: Leading figures, not thinkers: Pope Innocent III solidified Guelph ascendancy; the Cerchi led White Guelphs and the Donati Black Guelphs in Florence.

name: Ghibellines
origin_note: Names from Welf and Waiblingen came into Italian use in the late 12th century and 'solidified' as faction labels 'in Florence by 1215'; Ghibellines backed the Holy Roman Emperor
plain: The medieval Italian faction that sided with the Holy Roman Emperor against the pope, strong in Pisa and Siena.
summary: Pro-imperial faction of Italian city-states from about 1215 into the 14th century; won at Montaperti in 1260 under Sienese leadership.

rationale.christianity: Catholic factions opposing papal temporal power, not the faith (Grokipedia, Guelphs and Ghibellines).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: No real link to Enlightenment liberalism.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Alignments were 'pragmatic rather than doctrinal', driven by feuds and trade (Grokipedia, Guelphs and Ghibellines).
rationale.hierarchy: Backed imperial overlordship and feudal hierarchy over communal autonomy.
rationale.nationalism: No documented relation (predates Nationalism).

places.note: Kept a consistent Ghibelline orientation, seeking imperial support in Mediterranean trade.
A Ghibelline bastion; routed Florentine Guelphs at Montaperti in 1260.
Turned from Guelph influence under the Torriani to the Visconti after 1277.

parent_note: Parentless: the map has no Holy Roman Empire idea to serve as parent.

name: Maoism
origin_note: Held by 1937–1938 (On Practice and On Contradiction, 1937; Mao's 1938 Sixth Plenum report on the Sinification of Marxism); developed at the CCP's Yan'an base (1935–1945) and the 1942–1945 Rectification Campaign; the Seventh Congress at Yan'an, April 23–June 11, 1945, wrote Mao Zedong Thought into the party constitution
plain: Mao Zedong's version of Marxism-Leninism for a peasant country: rural revolution, the mass line, people's war and continuing class struggle.
summary: Marxism-Leninism adapted by Mao at Yan'an and codified in 1945; official CCP ideology, revised by the 1981 resolution; exported to insurgencies abroad.

rationale.christianity: A general anti-religious campaign: the Four Olds drive 'led to the ransacking of temples' and attacked old culture (Grokipedia, Maoism).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Rejects liberal pluralism for party rule and continuing class struggle (Grokipedia, Maoism).
rationale.marxism: Defined as a variant of Marxism-Leninism (Grokipedia, Maoism).
rationale.critical_theory: Separate lineage; overlaps only through Western student Maoism in the 1960s.
rationale.confucianism: Mao favored Legalist state-building over Confucian moralism (Grokipedia, Maoism).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Stresses practice and peasant conditions over doctrine, though built on dialectics.
rationale.hierarchy: One-party rule and personality cult, alongside mass-line egalitarian rhetoric (Grokipedia, Maoism).
rationale.nationalism: Sinified Marxism to Chinese conditions and backed national liberation struggles in the Third World.

places.note: Guiding ideology of the CCP since 1945; the 1981 resolution kept it while criticizing Mao's later errors.
Template for India's Naxalite movement (Grokipedia, Maoism).
Template for Peru's Shining Path (Grokipedia, Maoism).
Template for Nepal's Maoist rebellion (Grokipedia, Maoism).

leninism.note: 'A variant of Marxism-Leninism' adapting Marxist theory to a semi-feudal, agrarian society.

marxism.note: The Seventh Congress defined it as the integration of Marxist-Leninist theory with Chinese practice.

party_alignment_cn.note: Bloc: still the party's charter doctrine and venerated, though its core tenets were superseded after 1978; neo-Maoist strand sits with LEFT.

parent_note: Assessments are contested: the page reports unification, land reform and gains alongside famine and Cultural Revolution deaths; the CCP's 1981 resolution judged merits primary, errors secondary.

name: Samurai warrior ethos
origin_note: Warrior ethics of service to lords and prowess in battle 'trace to the Kamakura period (1185–1333)', but 'no unified bushido code existed' then
plain: The unwritten code of Japan's medieval warriors: service to a lord, courage in battle and an honorable death, before anyone called it bushido.
summary: Medieval Japanese warrior norms from the Kamakura period on; loyalty was 'often conditional on mutual benefit'. No single written code; later systematized as bushido.

rationale.stoicism: Stoic acceptance of death is a parallel, not a lineage (Grokipedia, Samurai).
rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: No real link to Enlightenment liberalism.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: Blended 'Confucian hierarchy' into warrior duty (Grokipedia, Samurai).
rationale.buddhism: Zen shaped warrior mindset from the early 13th century (Grokipedia, Bushido).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: A practical code of conduct in battle and service, not a theory.
rationale.hierarchy: Built on lord-vassal duty, though loyalty was often conditional (Grokipedia, Bushido).
rationale.nationalism: No documented relation (predates Nationalism).

aliases: Way of the bow and horse

places.note: Seat of the Kamakura shogunate, 1185–1333, when the warrior class took power.
Warring States era, 1336–1603, saw piecemeal codification attempts in house codes.

confucian_ethics.note: The samurai ethic blended 'Confucian hierarchy, Zen resilience, and indigenous valor'.

zen.note: 'Zen Buddhism's introduction in the early 13th century further shaped warrior mindset', promoting acceptance of death.

name: Bushido
origin_note: The term and 'systematized tenets emerged piecemeal in Edo-era (1603–1868) texts'; Yamaga Sokō (1622–1685) 'first systematically employed' it in The Way of the Samurai (Bushidō, 'circa 1665'); his teaching earned exile in 1666
plain: The 'way of the warrior' as Edo-period scholars wrote it down for samurai in peacetime: loyalty, rectitude, readiness for death.
summary: Edo-period systematization of the warrior ethic by Yamaga Sokō and Hagakure (1709–1716), for a samurai class turned administrators; varied by domain.

rationale.stoicism: Calm resolve unto death resembles Stoic themes; a parallel only.
rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: No real link to Enlightenment liberalism.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: Yamaga's Way was shaped by 'Confucian hierarchies' and service through scholarship (Grokipedia, Bushido).
rationale.buddhism: Hagakure 'blended Zen fatalism' into the ideal; a minor strand (Grokipedia, Bushido).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Written ethics for conduct, more systematic than the medieval ethos.
rationale.hierarchy: Stresses 'unyielding lord-vassal bonds' (Grokipedia, Bushido).
rationale.nationalism: No documented relation (predates Nationalism).

places.note: Yamaga Sokō taught the warrior's Way and was exiled in 1666 for critiquing shogunal orthodoxy.
Hagakure was compiled for the Nabeshima clan, 1709–1716.

samurai_ethos.note: Edo writers drew on medieval warrior norms 'amid peacetime reflections on martial heritage'.

neo_confucianism.note: Yamaga's Way was 'influenced by Confucian hierarchies', though he critiqued shogunal orthodoxy.

zen.note: Hagakure 'blended Zen fatalism with Shinto purity' (Grokipedia, Bushido).

shinto.note: Edo bushido was influenced by 'Shinto reverence for purity and ancestry'; Hagakure 'blended Zen fatalism with Shinto purity'.

parent_note: Recorders are not parents: Inoue Tetsujirō and Nitobe Inazō later wrote it up; see meiji_bushido.

name: Meiji Bushido
origin_note: Nitobe Inazō 'composed Bushido: The Soul of Japan in English in 1899'; published in 1900 in Philadelphia; Inoue Tetsujirō also wrote on bushido in the 1890s
plain: The modern image of bushido as a national samurai chivalry, written for Japanese schools and Western readers after the samurai class was gone.
summary: Late-Meiji reworking of bushido as loyalty to the emperor and a Japanese chivalry (Nitobe, 1899); scholars call it 'an adaptive invention'.

rationale.christianity: Nitobe was a Christian, Quaker-leaning intellectual comparing bushido with chivalry (Grokipedia, Nitobe Inazō).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Framed to aid 'modernization and diplomacy' with the West (Grokipedia, Bushido).
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: Kept Confucian loyalty and filial piety, now aimed at the emperor (Grokipedia, Bushido).
rationale.buddhism: Keeps Zen themes as heritage; a minor strand.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: An idealized national ethic, more abstract than lived Edo practice.
rationale.hierarchy: Redirected loyalty to the emperor as the head of the nation (Grokipedia, Bushido).
rationale.nationalism: Nitobe's Bushido aligned samurai virtues 'with Meiji nationalism' for an international audience.

places.note: Amplified in early 20th-century education, which claimed ancient origins for it.
Nitobe's book was published in Philadelphia in 1900 for Western readers.

bushido.note: Drew 'on Edo texts' but redirected loyalty from daimyo to the emperor.

nationalism.note: A work 'blending historical motifs with Meiji-era nationalism'.

parent_note: Place approximate: Japan, where Nitobe and Inoue held and taught the idea. Philadelphia (Leeds & Biddle, 1900) is only where the book was recorded in print.

name: Mito school
origin_note: The slogan sonnō jōi was 'first articulated by scholar Aizawa Seishisai in his 1825 treatise Shinron' in the Mito domain; the Mito school had earlier roots
plain: Scholars of the Mito domain who called the country to revere the emperor and expel foreigners, and named Japan's unique polity, kokutai.
summary: Late-Edo school of the Mito domain that framed kokutai as divinely ordained and coined the program sonnō jōi in Aizawa's Shinron (1825).

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Called for expelling Western powers (Grokipedia, Sonnō jōi).
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: 'Rooted in Neo-Confucian and Shinto principles' (Grokipedia, Sonnō jōi).
rationale.buddhism: Nativist and Confucian; no Buddhist grounding in the sources.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Built a theory of an eternal national essence, kokutai (Grokipedia, Kokutai).
rationale.hierarchy: Required 'loyalty to the throne' as divinely ordained (Grokipedia, Kokutai).
rationale.nationalism: Its sonno joi slogan is read by some historians as 'defensive nationalism', though the page stresses Confucian roots.

aliases: Revere the emperor, expel the barbarians

places.note: The Mito domain's intellectual circle first articulated the slogan in 1825.
Domain-wide calls for action against Western ships in 1863; pivot after the 1864 punitive expedition.

neo_confucianism.note: Aizawa's 'anti-foreign nativism' was 'rooted in Neo-Confucian and Shinto principles'.

shinto.note: The same line names Shinto as the second root.

kokugaku.note: Nativist (Kokugaku) efforts 'laid proto-kokutai foundations'; the Mito thinkers 'advanced this'.

parent_note: No Grokipedia page for Mito school (404); built from the Sonnō jōi and Kokutai pages. Founding of the school under Tokugawa Mitsukuni is not sourced here, so the node dates from Shinron.

name: State Shinto
origin_note: The government's sponsorship and ideological use of Shinto ran 'from the Meiji Restoration in 1868 until its abolition in 1945'; the label Kokka Shintō is mostly retrospective
plain: The Meiji state's use of shrine Shinto as a national civic rite, centered on the emperor as a descendant of the kami.
summary: State-run shrine Shinto from 1868 to 1945, set apart from sect Shinto in 1882 and treated as non-religious civic duty; abolished by the Shinto Directive.

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: No real link to Enlightenment liberalism.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: Moral education for subjects drew on Confucian loyalty; secondary.
rationale.buddhism: Built on the 'Separation from Buddhism' of shrines (Grokipedia, State Shinto).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Ritual and institutional; avoided 'doctrinal innovation' (Grokipedia, State Shinto).
rationale.hierarchy: A ranked shrine system centered on the emperor's divine descent (Grokipedia, State Shinto).
rationale.nationalism: A tool for ethnic nationalism and imperial legitimacy, embedding loyalty and nationalism in daily life via shrine rites.

places.note: Hierarchical network of state-ranked shrines until the 1945 Shinto Directive.
Promoted in the colonies of Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria.
Promoted in the colonies of Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria.

shinto.note: 'Transformed traditional shrine rituals and folk beliefs into a framework for national cohesion'.

kokugaku.note: 'The revival of Shinto began' with Kokugaku; Hirata Atsutane gave it 'a more activist and nationalistic framework'.

parent_note: Place: Tokyo as seat of the Meiji government; the page dates the system nationally, not to one city.

name: Kokutai
origin_note: Held as state doctrine from the Meiji Restoration of 1868, 'drawing on Mito school ideas'; Aizawa framed it in 1825; the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education and Kokutai no Hongi (1937) recorded it
plain: The idea that Japan is a unique 'national body' headed by an unbroken line of divine emperors, which no constitution could change.
summary: Doctrine of Japan's eternal, emperor-centered national polity: Meiji state creed from 1868, enforced by the 1925 Peace Preservation Law, set out in Kokutai no Hongi (1937).

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Kokutai no Hongi rejected 'individualistic Western liberalism' (Grokipedia, Kokutai).
rationale.marxism: The 1925 Peace Preservation Law aimed at socialists in its name (Grokipedia, Kokutai).
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: The Rescript mandated 'filial piety toward the emperor as the basis for civic duty' (Grokipedia, Kokutai).
rationale.buddhism: Shinto- and Confucian-based; Buddhism absorbed as foreign influence (Grokipedia, Statism in Shōwa Japan).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: An eternal national essence set apart from any form of government (Grokipedia, Kokutai).
rationale.hierarchy: The emperor as sacred, inviolable head of the national family (Grokipedia, Japanese nationalism).
rationale.nationalism: Core of Japanese nationalism from 1868, framing Japan as a divine realm under an unbroken imperial line.

places.note: Taught in schools through the 1890 Rescript; a 1925 law 'criminalized organizations or ideologies deemed to alter the kokutai'.

mito_school.note: Mito thinkers framed 'kokutai as an eternal, divinely ordained national essence' in Shinron (1825).

state_shinto.note: Its 'Integration with State Shinto and Emperor Veneration' is treated as core.

confucian_ethics.note: The 1890 Rescript enshrined 'filial piety, loyalty' and drew 'from Confucian and samurai precedents' (Grokipedia, Bushido).

parent_note: Place: Tokyo as seat of the Meiji government; the page dates the doctrine nationally, not to one city. Recorders are not parents: the Rescript and Kokutai no Hongi are documents that set it down.

name: Fukoku kyōhei
origin_note: 'The central slogan of Japan's Meiji government after the 1868 Restoration'; the phrase derives from the Chinese Zhan Guo Ce
plain: The Meiji program 'rich country, strong army': adopt Western industry, schools and armies fast to keep Japan from being colonized.
summary: Meiji modernization creed from 1868: conscription (1873), state industry and selective Western adoption to reach 'equal international standing'.

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: 'Selective Western adoption' in technology and governance, not liberal rights (Grokipedia, Fukoku kyōhei).
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.darwinism: Framed as survival against 'Western encroachment'; no Darwinian sources on the page.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: Legalist-style state power 'at the expense of moral or ritualistic ideals favored by Confucians' (Grokipedia, Fukoku kyōhei).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: A practical policy slogan for industry and armies.
rationale.hierarchy: State-directed, oligarch-led reform under imperial authority (Grokipedia, Fukoku kyōhei).
rationale.nationalism: National strengthening program; its emphasis on 'national homogeneity' and centralization; emperor-centric nationalism persisted.

places.note: Guided reform from 1868; universal male conscription began in 1873.

legalism.note: The slogan comes from Warring States 'fuguo qiangbing', linked on the page to Legalists like Shang Yang; a borrowed phrase, not a school.

parent_note: Replaced 'the prior sonnō jōi emphasis on isolation' (Grokipedia, Fukoku kyōhei): a successor to mito_school, not its child. Place: Tokyo as seat of the Meiji government; the page dates the program nationally, not to one city.

name: Taishō democracy
origin_note: 'The era of political liberalization and party ascendancy in Japan spanning approximately 1912 to 1932'; Yoshino Sakuzō argued for minponshugi
plain: The early 20th-century push in Japan for party cabinets, wider voting and government by public opinion within the imperial constitution.
summary: Liberal constitutional current of about 1912–1932: Yoshino's minponshugi, party cabinets from 1918, male suffrage in 1925; checked by the 1925 Peace Preservation Law.

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Pushed 'civil liberties' and party government, within 'persistent imperial prerogatives' (Grokipedia, Taishō Democracy).
rationale.marxism: Coexisted with labor agitation and debate on 'social equity' (Grokipedia, Taishō Democracy).
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Concrete constitutional and electoral reform.
rationale.hierarchy: Challenged 'oligarchic dominance' but kept the emperor (Grokipedia, Taishō Democracy).
rationale.nationalism: No documented relation.

places.note: Hara Takashi formed the first commoner-led party cabinet in 1918.

enlightenment_liberalism.note: 'Political liberalization' and 'movements for constitutional reform' against oligarchic rule.

parent_note: Minobe's organ theory (Kenpō kōwa, 1912) is on the Statism in Shōwa Japan page. Place Tokyo is the Diet's seat; the page dates the movement nationally.

name: Pan-Asianism
origin_note: Originated 'in late 19th-century Japan'; the Kōakai (Exalt Asia Society), 'founded in 1880', institutionalized it; Okakura wrote 'Asia is one' in 1903
plain: The call for Asian peoples to stand together against Western empires, which Japan later used to justify its own rule over Asia.
summary: Ideal of Asian unity from 1880s Japan (Kōakai, Okakura's 'Asia is one'), taken up by Sun Yat-sen; turned to justify expansion in the 1930s.

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Early anti-imperialist and partly republican (Tarui), but against Western dominance.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: Saw Asia as 'a hierarchical family of nations' in Confucian terms (Grokipedia, Pan-Asianism).
rationale.buddhism: Okakura drew 'on Buddhist and Confucian motifs' (Grokipedia, Pan-Asianism).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Asia as 'a cohesive spiritual entity', an abstract civilizational idea (Grokipedia, Pan-Asianism).
rationale.hierarchy: Early equality talk gave way to Japanese leadership (Grokipedia, Pan-Asianism).
rationale.islam: Only tactical contact with pan-Islamists (Okawa, c.1918-1923), an elite discourse rather than a mass movement; no real link to Islam.
rationale.nationalism: Regional solidarity rather than 'modern nationalism alone', but later infused 'with nationalist urgency'.

places.note: Kōakai in 1880; momentum after the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905.
Sun Yat-sen's Greater Asianism, including his 1924 Kobe speech.
Tagore engaged and critiqued it (Grokipedia, Pan-Asianism).

confucian_ethics.note: 'Incorporated Confucian principles to conceptualize Asia as a hierarchical family of nations'.

parent_note: Place approximate: the page does not give the Kōakai's founding city; Tokyo is used as the likely seat. Okakura's 1903 book is the classic text.

name: Shōwa statism
origin_note: Precursor: 'the 1919 founding of Yūzonsha by Kita Ikki and Ōkawa Shūmei'; Kita drafted his Outline Plan in Shanghai in 1919; state ideology 'from the late 1920s onward' to 1945
plain: The 1920s–1945 Japanese creed that put the emperor's state above parties and individuals, backed military rule and expansion in Asia.
summary: Kokkashugi: ultranationalist, militarist state ideology of Imperial Japan, late 1920s–1945; Kita Ikki, Kōdōha, Kokutai no Hongi, the 1940 Co-Prosperity Sphere.

rationale.christianity: No real link to Christianity.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Rejected 'Western liberal individualism' and dissolved parties (Grokipedia, Statism in Shōwa Japan).
rationale.marxism: Anti-communist, though Kita's plan nationalized industry and land (Grokipedia, Ikki Kita).
rationale.darwinism: Autarky and expansion framed as survival amid 'encirclement' (Grokipedia, Statism in Shōwa Japan).
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.confucianism: 'Integrated Confucian hierarchies' into a 'family state' (Grokipedia, Statism in Shōwa Japan).
rationale.buddhism: Buddhism treated as a foreign import absorbed by kokutai; Kita drew on Nichiren (Grokipedia, Ikki Kita).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: Mythic kokutai doctrine plus practical total mobilization.
rationale.hierarchy: 'Absolute authority of the state under the Emperor' (Grokipedia, Statism in Shōwa Japan).
rationale.nationalism: Kita Ikki and Okawa's Yuzonsha was a 'radical nationalist organization'; Kita blended socialism with anti-liberal nationalism.

places.note: Ruling ideology; the Imperial Rule Assistance Association dissolved the parties in 1940.
Victories such as the Manchurian Incident of 1931 were claimed as its fruits.
The Co-Prosperity Sphere expanded to Indochina, the Dutch East Indies and beyond.

kokutai.note: 'Emphasizing the kokutai', systematized in the 1937 Kokutai no Hongi.

nationalism.note: A 'syncretic political ideology' blending 'ultranationalism' and militarism; unlike European popular nationalism.

pan_asianism.note: Ideologues framed the Co-Prosperity Sphere 'as an extension of pan-Asianism'.

meiji_bushido.note: Araki's kōdō 'fused bushidō ethics with emperor-centric statism'.

parent_note: Not linked to fascism: 'retrospectively likened to fascism by some scholars', it 'lacked self-identification as such' (Grokipedia, Statism in Shōwa Japan). Kita's 1919 draft was published in 1923.

name: Kyoto School
origin_note: Nishida Kitarō began his system 'in his maiden work, An Inquiry into the Good, published in 1911', which won him a post at Kyoto University (SEP, Kyoto School)
plain: Japanese philosophers at Kyoto who used Western philosophy to think through Zen ideas, above all 'absolute nothingness'.
summary: School of Nishida, Tanabe and Nishitani at Kyoto from 1911: 'pure experience' and 'absolute nothingness'; wartime symposia drew charges of nationalism.

rationale.christianity: Ueda read Zen 'in relation to Meister Eckhart'; Christian mysticism as a dialogue partner (SEP).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: No real link to Enlightenment liberalism.
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.nietzsche: Nishitani read nothingness in Nietzsche and Heidegger, finding 'residues of an ontological bias' (SEP, Kyoto School).
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.daoism: SEP traces 'Buddhist and Daoist sources of the idea of absolute nothingness'.
rationale.buddhism: Built on 'Mahāyāna Buddhist doctrines, particularly Zen' (Grokipedia, Kyoto School).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Not carried in an ironic tone.
rationale.abstraction: A metaphysics of 'absolute nothingness', among the most abstract on the map.
rationale.hierarchy: Philosophical, not political; wartime nationalism charges are contested (SEP).
rationale.nationalism: Mixed: its wartime writings were co-opted by extreme nationalism they tried to reorient; scholars still dispute complicity.

places.note: Centered on Kyoto Imperial University's philosophy department.
Abe Masao contributed 'to inter-religious dialogue in North America'.

zen.note: Integrated Western methods 'with Mahāyāna Buddhist doctrines, particularly Zen'; Nishida kept 'a dedicated practice of Zen' (SEP).

phenomenology.note: Integrated 'phenomenology and idealism'; Nishitani studied with Heidegger 1937–1939.

hegelian_dialectic.note: 'Adapts Hegelian dialectics' into a self-negating process.

parent_note: Wartime role contested: 1942 'Overcoming Modernity' and 1943 world-history roundtables (Grokipedia, Kyoto School); SEP reports critics citing 'a nationalistic character'. No edge to showa_statism.

name: Psychoanalysis
origin_note: Breuer and Freud's Studies on Hysteria is 'a 1895 clinical monograph co-authored by Viennese physicians'; Freud's April 21, 1896, lecture 'The Aetiology of Hysteria' set out the seduction theory, dropped by 1897
plain: Freud's theory that hidden wishes and memories, mostly sexual and from childhood, drive what people do, and his talking cure for bringing them to light.
summary: Freud's theory and therapy of the unconscious: repression, dreams as wish-fulfillment, infantile sexuality and the Oedipus complex; organized in Vienna from 1902.

rationale.christianity: The Future of an Illusion (1927) calls religion 'an illusion rooted in human helplessness' (Grokipedia, Sigmund Freud).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: A rationalist science of mind; a 'materialistic framework' shaped his early rejection of metaphysics (Grokipedia, Psychoanalysis).
rationale.marxism: No real link to Marxism.
rationale.darwinism: Treats drives as biological instincts (Eros, Thanatos); a naturalist frame more than a Darwinian lineage.
rationale.nietzsche: Freud granted Nietzsche's intuitions matched his findings but said he avoided reading him (Autobiographical Study, 1925).
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).
rationale.judaism: Freud was of Jewish birth but treated all religion as illusion; Moses and Monotheism is a late work (Grokipedia, Sigmund Freud).
rationale.romanticism: The unconscious had Romantic precursors in Schelling (Grokipedia, Unconscious mind); Freud framed his own work as science.
rationale.nationalism: No real link to nationalism.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Makes its case directly, without ironic distance.
rationale.abstraction: Clinical and drive-based; the mind as a system of instinctual energies, not ideal forms.
rationale.hierarchy: Civilization needs the 'repression of primal instincts' via superego (Grokipedia, Sigmund Freud); not a political creed.

places.note: Freud's Psychological Wednesday Society (1902) became the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society by 1908.
After the 1909 lectures, U.S. psychoanalytic clinics appeared 'by the 1910s'.
Freud emigrated to London in 1938 amid Nazi persecution.

romanticism.note: 'Within German Romanticism', Schelling 'introduced the Unbewusstes (unconscious)'; the page treats this as background to Freud's model, not a source he drew on.

will_to_power.note: Freud: Nietzsche's 'guesses and intuitions often agree in the most astonishing way' with psychoanalysis, but 'was for a long time avoided by me' (1925).

parent_note: Schopenhauer has no node; the Schopenhauer page says his will 'resonated with' Freud's id, 'though Freud cited Schopenhauer sparingly', and Freud wrote 'I read Schopenhauer very late in my life' (Autobiographical Study, SE 20:59–60, transcribed at freudpage.info). No edge.

name: Tech right
origin_note: Dated to its earliest program statement, Andreessen's Techno-Optimist Manifesto (October 16, 2023); roots in libertarian Silicon Valley circles of the 2010s; became a visible faction after tech leaders endorsed Trump following the July 13, 2024, assassination attempt
plain: Silicon Valley investors and founders who joined the Republican coalition in 2024 to push for faster AI, crypto, less regulation and a leaner government.
summary: Pro-technology right of Silicon Valley investors (Thiel, Andreessen, Musk, Sacks): deregulation, AI and crypto, merit, skilled immigration; allied with Trump from 2024.

rationale.christianity: No documented relation; secular in idiom.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Free markets, free speech and 'enlightenment values of free discourse' (Andreessen, 2023); Thiel doubts democracy (2009).
rationale.marxism: Andreessen's manifesto names 'statism, authoritarianism, collectivism, central planning, socialism' as the enemy (2023).
rationale.darwinism: 'We believe in competition, because we believe in evolution' (Andreessen, Techno-Optimist Manifesto, 2023).
rationale.nietzsche: Andreessen lists Nietzsche as a patron saint and casts the Last Man and ressentiment as the enemy (2023).
rationale.critical_theory: Critiques 'woke' culture in tech firms for putting diversity quotas and content moderation over engineering (Grokipedia, Tech right).
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).
rationale.romanticism: Andreessen: 'We believe in the romance of technology, of industry', quoting Marinetti; a Futurist, not folk, romance.
rationale.nationalism: Wants a technologically strong America against China, yet backs H-1B skilled immigration against nativists (Grokipedia, Tech right).
rationale.humor: Allied e/acc culture spread through playful, pseudonymous posts on X (Grokipedia, Effective accelerationism).
rationale.irony: Some overlap with ironic 'Dark MAGA' online aesthetics (Grokipedia, Effective accelerationism); leaders mostly argue straight.
rationale.abstraction: Judges by output and productivity; Andreessen's 'material philosophy' (2023) means material abundance and progress, not matter over mind.
rationale.hierarchy: Embraces 'inequality as a byproduct of meritocratic progress' (Grokipedia, Tech right); Thiel: freedom and democracy may not be compatible.

places.note: A network of executives and investors 'largely based in Silicon Valley' (Grokipedia, Tech right).
From 2025 through DOGE, Sacks's AI and crypto post and allied appointees in the Trump administration.

libertarianism.note: Grokipedia: the Tech right 'draws from a tech-centric libertarianism'; Thiel's 2009 'The Education of a Libertarian' marks the handoff.

effective_accelerationism.note: Andreessen put 'e/acc' in his profiles; after Trump's 2024 win e/acc 'aligned closely with the second Trump administration's deregulatory agenda'.

neoreaction.note: Grokipedia: Thiel 'drew on neoreactionary critiques of bureaucratic stagnation' to fund exit ventures; how far this shapes the faction is disputed.

maga.note: Coalition partner, not ancestor: tech leaders endorsed Trump in July 2024; by 2026 members 'questioned alignments with broader MAGA elements'.

party_alignment.note: Aligned with the Trump administration from 2025; 2026 rifts with MAGA over H-1B, ICE and Bannon; Andreessen says techno-optimists are 'not necessarily right wing'.

parent_note: No accelerationism edge: the handoff runs through effective_accelerationism. No cypherpunks edge: The Sovereign Individual (1997), which Thiel prefaced in 2020, is the closer source and has no node.

name: Wilsonianism (liberal internationalism)
origin_note: Dated to Wilson's April 2, 1917, war message, which called the war a crusade 'to make the world safe for democracy'; a doctrine 'originating with President Woodrow Wilson during World War I', later 'rooted in Wilson's Fourteen Points speech of January 1918'
plain: Woodrow Wilson's idea that America should spread democracy, back national self-rule and build a league of nations so that collective security replaces the balance of power.
summary: Wilson's World War I program: democracy promotion, self-determination, open diplomacy and collective security through a League of Nations; revived in later US policy.

rationale.christianity: Wilson's Presbyterian upbringing shaped 'a worldview integrating religious ethics with governance' (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Universal democracy, consent and collective security; echoes 'Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty' (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).
rationale.marxism: A liberal rival to revolutionary socialism after 1917; not defined by anticommunism the way later Cold War strands were.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).
rationale.nationalism: National self-determination is a core plank: Points 9–14 sought polities for nationalities under imperial rule (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Makes its case directly, without ironic distance.
rationale.abstraction: Builds world order 'on moral and legalistic foundations rather than balance-of-power realism' (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).
rationale.hierarchy: Favors law, open covenants and collective security among nations over great-power spheres (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).

places.note: Wilson's Fourteen Points (January 1918) and war message (1917) set the doctrine as US policy.
Wilson pressed the program at the Paris Peace Conference, the program 'inspiring the League of Nations covenant'.
The UN Charter (1945) directly inheriting the League of Nations' structure for collective security; the UN sits in New York.

enlightenment_liberalism.note: Self-determination 'derived from consent-based governance, echoing Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty but applied internationally'.

calvinism.note: Wilson grew up in 'a strict Calvinist environment' as a Presbyterian minister's son; the page ties this to his moral view of governance.

parent_note: Liberal internationalism is merged here as an alias: Grokipedia says it 'crystallized as a coherent doctrine during World War I under U.S. President Woodrow Wilson'. Its 19th-century free-trade forerunners are not split out.

name: Cold War liberal anticommunism
origin_note: Americans for Democratic Action was 'founded in 1947' by Eleanor Roosevelt, Hubert Humphrey, Arthur Schlesinger Jr., Reinhold Niebuhr and others 'to advance non-communist progressive policies'; Truman announced his doctrine on March 12, 1947; Schlesinger's The Vital Center followed in 1949
plain: Postwar Democrats who kept the New Deal at home and fought communism abroad: Truman's containment, the ADA and Schlesinger's 'vital center' between left and right extremes.
summary: Postwar liberalism that paired New Deal welfare with anticommunist containment; Truman, ADA (1947), Schlesinger's Vital Center (1949), later Scoop Jackson.

rationale.christianity: Reinhold Niebuhr, a Protestant theologian, co-founded ADA (Grokipedia, ADA); the movement itself was secular in program.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Vital-center liberalism stressed 'individual integrity, pluralism' and democratic freedom (Grokipedia, Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.).
rationale.marxism: Founded 'to advance non-communist progressive policies' (Grokipedia, ADA); containment of Soviet communism is its core.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).
rationale.nationalism: Patriotic defense of the free world; Jackson stressed 'military strength' against Soviet expansion (Grokipedia, Henry M. Jackson).
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Makes its case directly, without ironic distance.
rationale.abstraction: Schlesinger grounded it in 'empirical recognition of human imperfection' (Grokipedia, Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.).
rationale.hierarchy: Backed a strong national-security state abroad while extending welfare and labor protections at home (Grokipedia, Henry M. Jackson).

places.note: Truman's March 12, 1947 address committed aid to Greece and Turkey against communist pressure.
Jackson's Coalition for a Democratic Majority (May 1972) sought 'to reclaim the party from New Left influences'.

new_deal_liberalism.note: ADA's founders, New Deal Democrats, organized after FDR's death to keep liberalism non-communist; The Vital Center defended the New Deal against totalitarianism.

wilsonianism.note: The Truman Doctrine framed containment 'as an extension of Wilsonian self-determination and democratic expansion against Soviet influence'.

parent_note: Grokipedia has no 'Cold War liberalism' or 'Vital Center' article; the node rests on ADA, Schlesinger, Truman Doctrine, Jackson and Neoconservatism pages. Reinhold Niebuhr is an ADA founder but has no node.

name: Straussian political philosophy
origin_note: Dated to 1949, when Strauss took up a professorship at Chicago, where he 'cultivated a dedicated following of students through seminars focused on primary texts'; Natural Right and History (1953) set out his defense of 'timeless natural right'; 'By the time of Strauss's death in 1973, his students had formed a self-sustaining intellectual movement'
plain: Leo Strauss and his students: careful reading of Plato and the classics, a belief in natural right against modern relativism, and the claim that philosophers often wrote between the lines.
summary: Leo Strauss's recovery of classical political philosophy: natural right against historicism, esoteric reading of Plato, Farabi and Maimonides, and a school of students.

rationale.platonism: Defends 'timeless natural right grounded in reason and classical sources like Plato' (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.aristotelianism: Draws 'from Plato, Aristotle, and Machiavelli' for classical political philosophy (Grokipedia, Neoconservatism).
rationale.christianity: Frames the issue as philosophy versus revelation, Athens versus Jerusalem, without taking a Christian side (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Defends liberal democracy against totalitarianism but critiques modernity's break 'from classical natural right' (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.marxism: Treats modern historicism, Marxism's frame included, as leading to relativism and nihilism (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.nietzsche: Casts Nietzsche and Heidegger as the 'third wave' of modernity that ends in nihilism (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.critical_theory: Opposes historicist reduction of moral standards to 'cultural artifacts' (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss); no direct engagement.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: Read Al-Farabi as an esoteric writer and began with research on 'medieval Islamic philosophy' (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.judaism: Born to 'an observant Jewish family'; read Maimonides' Guide and wrote on philosophy versus revelation and Zionism (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.nationalism: No real link to nationalism.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Holds that philosophers wrote esoterically, hiding meanings beneath an exoteric surface (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.abstraction: Holds that enduring truths about human nature and the best regime 'can be discerned through reason' (Grokipedia, Neoconservatism).
rationale.hierarchy: Critics such as Drury see 'a stark natural hierarchy' of philosophers over the many; the page also records rebuttals (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).

places.note: Strauss taught there from 1949 and built a following of students around close reading of primary texts.
His students formed 'a self-sustaining intellectual movement' by 1973 that revived great-books education.

platonic_forms.note: Strauss defended 'timeless natural right grounded in reason and classical sources like Plato' and taught seminars on Plato's texts.

aristotelian_teleology.note: Strauss 'emphasized the enduring truths of classical political philosophy—drawing from Plato, Aristotle, and Machiavelli'.

falsafa.note: He began in 1932 researching 'medieval Islamic philosophy in Paris' and read Al-Farabi as veiling 'critiques of prophetic authority under apparent deference'.

name: Jacksonian democracy
origin_note: The Democratic-Republican remnants 'coalesced into what became known as the Democratic Party by 1828', the year of Jackson's election; his presidency ran 1829-1837
plain: A movement around Andrew Jackson that widened voting for white men, attacked the national bank and rewarded loyal supporters with office. It founded the Democratic Party.

rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).

american_republicanism.note: Jacksonians drew on 'Jeffersonian ideals of limited government and popular virtue' and the Democratic-Republicans' defense of the 'common man' (Grokipedia).

name: Free Soil

name: Milesian school
origin_note: Thales of Miletus, 'fl. c. 585 BCE', founds the school; he reputedly predicted the eclipse of May 28, 585 BCE
plain: The first Greek philosophers, from the city of Miletus. They tried to explain the world by natural causes instead of myths, each naming one basic stuff behind everything.
summary: Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes sought one first principle of all things (water, the boundless, air) and explained nature without divine intervention.

name: Eleatic school
origin_note: The school 'arose in the early fifth century BCE in the Greek colony of Elea'; Parmenides, its founder, is dated c. 515–450 BCE
plain: Greek philosophers from Elea, in southern Italy, who argued that reality is one thing that never changes. They held that change and motion are illusions of the senses.
summary: Parmenides' Way of Truth: what is must be one, whole, unborn and motionless. Zeno defended it with paradoxes of motion, and Melissus made Being infinite.

rationale.platonism: Parmenides 'directly influenced Plato's separation of sensible and intelligible worlds', and Plato named a dialogue after him.
rationale.aristotelianism: Aristotle answered the Eleatic denial of change with potentiality and actuality, and refuted Zeno's paradoxes.

name: Socratic philosophy
origin_note: Socrates (c. 469–399 BCE) questioned Athenians in public; he is documented in the 430s BCE, and Aristophanes' The Clouds (423 BCE) is the earliest depiction of him
plain: The way of thinking taught by Socrates in Athens. He questioned people to show what they did not know, and held that a good life comes from knowing what is right.
summary: Socrates' ethics and method: cross-examination (elenchus) to expose false beliefs, virtue as knowledge, professed ignorance and the examined life.

rationale.platonism: Plato's early dialogues preserve Socrates' method; Aristotle credits the Forms to Plato, not Socrates.
rationale.aristotelianism: Aristotle credits Socrates with seeking universal definitions in ethics.
rationale.stoicism: The Stoics, like the Cynics, cast themselves as continuators of Socrates' ethics.

name: Leninist theory of imperialism
origin_note: Lenin wrote Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism 'from January to June 1916 while exiled in Zurich'; it was first published in mid-1917 in Petrograd.
plain: Lenin's idea that empire is what capitalism turns into when big banks and monopolies run it. He said rich countries fight wars to divide up the world.
summary: Lenin (1916): monopoly and finance capital push rich states to export capital and carve up the world, so world war and colonies follow from capitalism itself.
aliases: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism

places.note: Became a foundational text of Soviet ideology after its 1917 publication.
Shaped revolutionary strategies in Russia, China and beyond, and anti-colonial movements.

leninism.note: Lenin's own pamphlet; it 'became a foundational text in Soviet ideology'.

marxism.note: Lenin adapted Hobson's and Hilferding's analyses 'to Marxist frameworks'.

parent_note: Also draws on two thinkers not on the map: Hilferding's Finance Capital (1910) and the liberal Hobson's Imperialism: A Study (1902).

name: Khomeinism
origin_note: Khomeini set out guardianship of the jurist 'in a series of lectures delivered in Najaf, Iraq, from January 21 to February 8, 1970', published that year as Islamic Government.
plain: Khomeini's teaching that, while the hidden Twelfth Imam is away, a top Islamic legal scholar should rule the state. It became the basis of Iran's government in 1979.
summary: Khomeini's doctrine (Najaf, 1970): a senior Shia jurist holds guardianship over the state until the Hidden Imam returns; enshrined in Iran's 1979 constitution.

places.note: Enshrined in Iran's 1979 Constitution, which makes the Supreme Leader the guardian jurist.
Iran aided the founding of Hezbollah in 1982 with guidance rooted in Khomeinist Shia Islamism.

islam.note: Described as 'a doctrine within Twelver Shia Islam'; many Shia scholars dispute its scope.

transcendent_theosophy.note: Khomeini's mentor Shahabadi taught him mysticism and theosophy 'drawing on thinkers like Mulla Sadra and Ibn Arabi'.

parent_note: Khomeini broke with the older Shia quietism that kept jurists out of rule; Twelver Shiism as such is not a separate node on the map.

name: Iranian nationalism
origin_note: Grokipedia dates its modern form to the late 19th century with Akhundzade and Kermani; Akhundzade's Letters of Kamal ud-Dowla were 'completed in 1865' in Tiflis.
plain: The idea that Iranians form one nation joined by the Persian language and a history going back to ancient Persia. Its early thinkers praised Iran before Islam.
summary: Iran as one nation rooted in pre-Islamic Persia and the Persian language: from Akhundzade's 1860s writings to Reza Shah's state-building and Mosaddegh's oil nationalization.

places.note: Became state policy under Reza Shah (1925-1941), who renamed Persia Iran in 1935.
Diaspora branches of the National Front and diaspora thinkers keep a secular nationalism alive.

nationalism.note: Akhundzade held 'a secular, progressive vision of vatan (homeland)', an early form of modern Iranian nationalism.

enlightenment_liberalism.note: Akhundzade fused reverence for ancient Iran 'with Enlightenment ideas of progress and rationalism'; he read Voltaire and Rousseau.

parent_note: Its founders also drew on European Orientalist scholarship and racial theories (Grokipedia, Iranian nationalism); no edge drawn to scientific racism (held).

name: Keynesian economics
origin_note: Keynes's General Theory appeared in February 1936, after his Cambridge lectures of 1933 and work with the 'Cambridge Circus' of younger economists.
plain: Keynes's idea that slumps happen when people and firms spend too little. He said governments should spend more in bad times to bring back jobs.
summary: Keynes (1936): too little total spending can leave an economy stuck with mass unemployment, so governments should boost demand, chiefly through spending.

places.note: Underpinned post-World War II demand management until the 1970s stagflation.
Post-Keynesian economics developed there around Joan Robinson, Nicholas Kaldor and Michal Kalecki.

parent_note: Keynes learned economics from Alfred Marshall and broke with the classical view that markets clear by themselves; neither Marshall's school nor classical economics is a node yet.
